name: Radicchio
notes: Cool-weather crop; heads form in cool temps. May bolt in heat

name: Endive
notes: Blanch inner leaves 2-3 weeks before harvest by tying outer leaves

name: Escarole
notes: Broad-leafed endive relative; blanch before harvest. Tolerates mild frost

name: Mache
notes: Extremely cold-hardy (to -5F). Ideal winter salad green. Does not tolerate heat

name: Cress
notes: One of the fastest greens from seed. Peppery flavor. Can grow indoors on windowsill

name: Purslane
notes: Succulent green rich in omega-3. Extremely drought tolerant. Seeds need light to germinate

name: Sorrel
notes: Lemony-flavored perennial green. One of first greens in spring. Remove flower stalks

name: Lamb's Quarters
notes: Highly nutritious wild edible. Harvest tender tips at 6-8 inches. Use like spinach

name: Watercress
notes: Semi-aquatic; keep soil constantly wet or grow in standing water. Peppery flavor

name: Malabar Spinach
notes: Tropical vine, not true spinach. Thrives in heat when real spinach bolts. Mucilaginous texture

name: New Zealand Spinach
notes: Heat-tolerant spinach substitute. Spreading ground-cover habit. Soak seeds overnight

name: Amaranth Greens
notes: Heat-loving green with nutritious leaves. Also produces edible grain if left to mature

name: Moringa
notes: Warm zones only. Fast-growing tree 10+ ft/year. Extremely nutritious leaves. Drought resistant

name: Fennel
notes: Bulbing fennel requires long cool season. Bolts in heat. Hill soil around bulbs

name: Celeriac
notes: Very long season; start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost. Seeds need light to germinate

name: Rutabaga
notes: Brassica family; flavor improves after frost. Plant midsummer for fall harvest

name: Parsnip
notes: Slow germinating; use only fresh seed. Flavor sweetens dramatically after frost

name: Daikon Radish
notes: Fall planting produces best roots. Roots can reach 18 inches. Also used as cover crop

name: Horseradish
notes: From root cuttings, not seed. Very vigorous; grow in containers to prevent spreading

name: Jicama
notes: Needs 150-180 frost-free days. Nick seed coat and soak before planting. Remove flowers for tubers

name: Taro
notes: Tropical, needs 200+ frost-free days. Loves wet boggy conditions. Must be cooked before eating

name: Ginger
notes: From rhizome pieces. Baby ginger at 4-6 months; mature at 8-10 months. Warm humid conditions

name: Turmeric
notes: From rhizome pieces. Prefers filtered light. Baby harvest at 4-6 months; mature at 8-10

name: Rhubarb
notes: Long-lived perennial (15+ yr). No harvest year 1. Needs winter chill. Only eat stalks; leaves toxic

name: Cassava
notes: Warm zones only. From stem cuttings. Needs 8-11 months frost-free. Must be cooked before eating

name: Edamame
notes: Direct sow after last frost when soil is 60F+. Harvest when pods are bright green and plump

name: Peanut
notes: Needs 120-150 frost-free days. Harvest when leaves yellow. Sandy soil preferred

name: Fava Bean
notes: Cool-season legume. Frost hardy to upper 20sF. Fixes nitrogen in soil. May need staking

name: Chickpea
notes: Cool-season legume. Fixes nitrogen. Prefers warm dry conditions for pod maturation

name: Lentil
notes: Cool-season legume. Fixes nitrogen. Allow pods to dry on plant. Reduce watering as pods mature

name: Winged Bean
notes: Tropical legume. All parts edible: pods, leaves, flowers, tubers. Needs trellis, vines 9-13 ft

name: Yard Long Bean
notes: Heat-loving vine bean. Needs sturdy trellis. Harvest pods at 10-12 inches for best flavor

name: Bok Choy
notes: Cool-season crop. Bolts in heat. Light frost improves flavor

name: Napa Cabbage
notes: Forms tight cylindrical heads. Best as fall crop. Frost tolerant to 26F when mature

name: Mizuna
notes: Fast-growing Asian mustard green. Slow to bolt compared to other greens

name: Tatsoi
notes: Extremely cold hardy to 15F. Spoon-shaped rosette. Baby leaf 21 days, full head 45

name: Komatsuna
notes: Japanese mustard spinach. Cold tolerant to 10-15F. Handles heat and cold better than most brassicas

name: Chinese Broccoli
notes: Thick stems with small florets. Harvest when flower buds just start to form

name: Broccoli Rabe
notes: Fast-growing cool-season crop. Harvest when buds are 1 inch wide. Frost tolerant to 25F

name: Romanesco
notes: Distinctive fractal spiral heads. Needs consistent moisture. Frost tolerant to 20F

name: Bitter Melon
notes: Tropical vine; needs trellis 5-6 ft. Scarify and soak seeds 24hrs. Harvest at 4-6 inches green

name: Luffa
notes: Needs 150+ warm frost-free days. Trellis 6+ ft. Harvest young for eating or mature for sponges

name: Chayote
notes: Plant entire sprouted fruit on side. Perennial zones 8+. Up to 100 fruits per vine

name: Calabash
notes: Harvest young for eating or mature for craft shells. Soak seeds 24 hrs. Strong trellis needed

name: Kabocha Squash
notes: Japanese winter squash with dense sweet flesh. Cure 5-7 days after harvest. Stores 2-3 months

name: Delicata Squash
notes: Winter squash with edible skin. Semi-bush habit. Shorter storage than other winter squash (2-3 mo)

name: Hubbard Squash
notes: Very large (15+ lbs). Long trailing vines need lots of space. Hard shell stores 6+ months

name: Patty Pan Squash
notes: Summer squash, compact bush habit. Harvest young at 2-3 inches. Very prolific producer

name: Snake Gourd
notes: Tropical vine; needs 5+ ft trellis for fruits to hang straight. Harvest young at 1-2 ft for eating

name: Tomatillo
notes: Requires 2+ plants for cross-pollination. Harvest when husks split and fruit fills husk

name: Ground Cherry
notes: Harvest when husks dry and papery, fruits yellow, drop to ground. Start indoors 6-8 weeks early

name: Gooseberry
notes: Thorny shrub. Fruit in 2-3 years. Tart berries for pies and preserves. Prune for air circulation

name: Currant
notes: Red, black, and white varieties. Very cold hardy. Tart fruit for jams and juice. Banned in some states

name: Elderberry
notes: Large shrub/small tree. Berries must be cooked before eating. Flowers also edible. Plant 2+ for pollination

name: Mulberry
notes: Fast-growing fruit tree. Very prolific; berries stain everything. Red, white, and black species

name: Pawpaw
notes: Native understory tree. Tropical-flavored custard fruit. Needs 2+ unrelated trees for pollination

name: American Persimmon
notes: Native tree with sweet fruit after frost. Astringent until fully ripe. Female tree needed for fruit

name: Hardy Kiwi
notes: Grape-sized smooth-skinned fruit. Needs sturdy trellis. Plant male and female vines for fruit

name: Honeyberry
notes: Also called haskap. Extremely cold hardy (-55F). Earliest fruit of the season. Plant 2+ varieties

name: Serviceberry
notes: Native shrub/tree. Sweet blueberry-like fruit in June. Also called saskatoon or juneberry

name: Goji Berry
notes: Semi-vine shrub. Drought tolerant once established. Produces midsummer to first frost

name: Cranberry
notes: Needs very acidic soil and consistent moisture. Ground-cover vine. About 1 lb per 4 sq ft established

name: Lingonberry
notes: Low evergreen ground cover. Two harvests: late summer and early fall. Needs acidic soil

name: Boysenberry
notes: Trailing canes need trellis. Cross of raspberry, blackberry, loganberry. Harvest May-July

name: Loganberry
notes: Raspberry-blackberry hybrid. Tart, excellent for pies and preserves. Harvest June-July

name: Marionberry
notes: Oregon signature berry. Intensely aromatic blackberry flavor. Trailing canes need trellis

name: Tayberry
notes: Scottish blackberry-raspberry cross. Sweeter and larger than loganberry. Harvest June-July

name: Dewberry
notes: Native trailing blackberry relative. Ripe late April-May, earlier than blackberries

name: Huckleberry
notes: Difficult to cultivate, slow growing. Needs acidic soil. Multiple species for different zones

name: Muscadine Grape
notes: Native Southern grape, needs humid climate. Thicker skin. Self-fertile varieties available

name: Quince
notes: Most varieties require cooking. Very fragrant golden fruit in late autumn. Good for preserves

name: Cape Gooseberry
notes: Golden berry in papery husk. Annual in frost zones, perennial frost-free. Prolific self-seeder

name: Prickly Pear
notes: Both pads (nopales) and fruit (tunas) edible. Extremely drought tolerant. Eastern species hardy to zone 4

name: Che Fruit
notes: Also called Mandarin Melon Berry. Fig-watermelon flavor. Seedless female trees bear without pollinator

name: Pomegranate
notes: Heat-loving, drought tolerant once established. Needs 120+ days above 85F for best fruit

name: Jujube
notes: Extremely drought tolerant. Flowers late avoiding frosts. Dormant trees hardy to -20F. Suckers can spread

name: Guava
notes: Tropical/subtropical. Damaged below 30F. Can be container-grown in colder zones and brought indoors

name: Loquat
notes: Tree hardy to 10F but flowers killed at 27F. Blooms fall/winter, fruit ripens spring

name: Dragonfruit
notes: Climbing cactus needing sturdy trellis. Plant from cuttings for faster fruit. Well-drained soil

name: Banana
notes: Needs 10-15 frost-free months to flower. Giant herbaceous plant. Heavy feeder

name: Lemon
notes: Most cold-sensitive common citrus. Fruit takes 6-9 months to ripen. Great in containers

name: Lime
notes: Most cold-sensitive citrus. Key limes very frost-tender; Persian limes slightly hardier

name: Orange
notes: Navel ripens winter, Valencia ripens late spring-summer. Dwarf varieties for containers

name: Grapefruit
notes: Largest citrus tree. Needs most heat for sweet fruit. Harvest late fall to spring

name: Kumquat
notes: Most cold-hardy citrus, survives to 18F. Eat whole including sweet rind. Compact growth

name: Meyer Lemon
notes: Lemon-mandarin hybrid. Sweeter than true lemons. More cold-tolerant (hardy to 21F). Great in containers

name: Satsuma
notes: Cold-hardiest true citrus mandarin (18-20F). Seedless, easy peel. Ripens Oct-Jan

name: Lemon Balm
notes: Perennial. Spreads aggressively, contain in pots. Lemon-scented leaves for tea and cooking

name: Chamomile
notes: German (annual) or Roman (perennial). Harvest flowers for tea when petals fold back

name: Stevia
notes: Natural sweetener 200-300x sugar. Annual in cold zones, perennial in zones 9+. Slow to germinate

name: Catnip
notes: Perennial. Attracts cats, repels mosquitoes and aphids. Vigorous spreader, deadhead to control

name: Hyssop
notes: Semi-evergreen perennial sub-shrub. Attracts pollinators. Minty-anise flavor for teas and cooking

name: Borage
notes: Annual with cucumber-flavored blue flowers. Attracts pollinators. Self-seeds readily

name: Comfrey
notes: Dynamic accumulator — chop-and-drop mulch. Propagated from root cuttings. Very difficult to remove once established

name: Feverfew
notes: Short-lived perennial. Medicinal for migraines. Self-seeds prolifically. Repels pests

name: Valerian
notes: Roots harvested fall of second year for medicinal use. Cold stratification improves germination

name: Echinacea
notes: Perennial. May take 2+ years from seed to bloom. Medicinal roots and flowers. Cold stratify seeds

name: Bee Balm
notes: Perennial. Prone to powdery mildew. Edible flowers taste like oregano/thyme. Attracts hummingbirds

name: Anise
notes: Annual. Needs 120+ frost-free days for seed harvest. Taproot does not transplant well

name: Caraway
notes: Biennial. Seeds harvested second year. Taproot does not transplant well. Hardy to -30F

name: Herb Fennel
notes: Grown for fronds and seeds, not bulb. Allelopathic — plant away from vegetable garden. Self-seeds

name: Epazote
notes: Traditional Mexican bean herb. Self-seeds aggressively. Surface sow, needs light to germinate

name: Shiso
notes: Japanese/Korean herb. Soak seeds 24 hrs before sowing. Red and green varieties. Annual in most zones

name: Summer Savory
notes: Annual known as the bean herb. Delicate flavor lighter than winter savory. Attracts honeybees

name: Winter Savory
notes: Perennial sub-shrub. More intense flavor than summer savory. Repels bean weevils and cabbage moths

name: French Tarragon
notes: Does NOT produce viable seed; propagate by division/cuttings. Classic anise flavor. Replace every 3-4 yr

name: Marjoram
notes: Tender perennial, annual in cold zones. Sweeter than oregano. Harvest before flowers for peak flavor

name: Lovage
notes: Perennial celery-flavored herb. Very large plant. Harvest leaves, stems, seeds, and roots

name: Angelica
notes: Biennial. Stems candied for confections. Seeds need light and cold to germinate. Grows very tall

name: Rue
notes: Perennial. Repels many pests. Causes skin irritation in some people. Bitter ornamental herb

name: Sweet Woodruff
notes: Woodland ground cover. Sweet vanilla-hay scent when dried. Used in May wine. Slow to establish

name: Salad Burnet
notes: Perennial. Young leaves taste of cucumber. Evergreen in mild winters. Remove flowers for leaf production

name: Sweet Cicely
notes: Perennial with anise-flavored leaves and sweet edible seeds. Needs cold stratification to germinate

name: Chervil
notes: Annual. Delicate anise-parsley flavor. Cool-season herb that bolts in heat. Succession sow

name: Curry Leaf
notes: Tropical tree essential in South Indian cooking. Not related to curry powder. Bring indoors in cold zones

name: Lemon Verbena
notes: Deciduous shrub. Strongest lemon fragrance of any herb. Loses leaves in winter even where hardy

name: Pineapple Sage
notes: Perennial in warm zones, annual elsewhere. Pineapple-scented leaves. Red tubular flowers attract hummingbirds

name: Mexican Oregano
notes: Different genus than true oregano (Lippia). Stronger, more citrusy. Essential in Tex-Mex and Latin cooking

name: Cuban Oregano
notes: Succulent herb (Coleus amboinicus). Strong oregano-thyme flavor. Easy from cuttings. Frost-tender

name: Vietnamese Coriander
notes: Heat-loving cilantro substitute. Grows in moist shade. Does not bolt. Propagate from cuttings

name: Culantro
notes: Stronger cilantro flavor, different plant (Eryngium). Surface sow, needs light. Heat-tolerant, won't bolt

name: Thai Basil
notes: Licorice-anise flavor, essential in Thai and Vietnamese cuisine. More heat-tolerant than sweet basil

name: Horehound
notes: Perennial bitter herb for cough remedies and candy. Very drought tolerant. Can be invasive

name: Wormwood
notes: Perennial. Strongly aromatic; repels insects. Allelopathic — keep away from edibles. Ornamental silver foliage

name: Tansy
notes: Perennial pest repellent plant. Toxic if ingested in large quantities. Very aggressive spreader

name: Pennyroyal
notes: Perennial ground cover. Strong mint-family insect repellent. Toxic if ingested — use externally only

name: Betony
notes: Perennial woodland herb. Traditional medicinal plant for headaches. Attracts pollinators

name: Meadowsweet
notes: Perennial. Sweet almond-vanilla scented flowers for teas and syrups. Source of aspirin compound

name: Costmary
notes: Perennial. Balsam-mint scent. Historic Bible leaf herb. Rarely flowers in cooler climates

name: Soapwort
notes: Perennial. Roots produce natural soap. Attractive pink flowers. Can be invasive; contain in pots

name: Elecampane
notes: Perennial. Large sunflower-like plant. Roots harvested year 2 for medicinal use. Camphor scent

name: Nasturtium
notes: Peppery edible flowers, leaves, and seed pods. Trap crop for aphids. Thrives in poor soil

name: Calendula
notes: Also called pot marigold. Petals for salads, soups (poor man's saffron). Medicinal for salves

name: Viola
notes: Mild sweet flowers for garnishing salads, desserts, drinks. Cool-season, blooms through winter zones 7-10

name: Sunflower
notes: Petals and seeds edible. Attracts pollinators and birds. Allelopathic; may inhibit nearby plants

name: Signet Marigold
notes: Tagetes tenuifolia. Citrus-tarragon flavor. Remove bitter white petal base. Repels whiteflies and nematodes

name: Hibiscus (Roselle)
notes: Calyces for tea, jams, agua de jamaica. Short-day plant blooms in fall. Start early in cold zones

name: Rose (Rugosa)
notes: Petals for rosewater, jams, teas. Hips very high in vitamin C. Extremely hardy and disease resistant

name: Dianthus
notes: Clove-scented edible petals for salads and desserts. Remove bitter white petal base before eating

name: Edible Chrysanthemum
notes: Shungiku/garland chrysanthemum. Leaves and flowers edible. Quick-growing cool-season crop. Bolts in heat

name: Daylily
notes: Flowers, buds, shoots, tubers all edible. Only Hemerocallis species — NOT true lilies. Each bloom lasts 1 day
